Explanation

Your application has hardcoded URLs that might correspond to services that are not accessible on Azure.

Review and ensure that the application is attempting to access URLs that would be available from Azure. You might need to migrate those services to Azure too, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.

If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premises, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.
Local or network IO operations detected
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.csLine 57
src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.csLine 57

Explanation

Your application has local or network IO operations.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move persistent I/O to storage mounts (Azure Files/UNC). Keep local writes to temp only; connect to external dependencies via private endpoints/VNet to reduce latency.

IO operations outside of the application folder might not be available on Azure App Service. Review and ensure IO APIs are attempting to access paths that will be available when your app is running on App Service sandbox. If you choose the containerized hosting option, your scenario still might be broken or have scalability issues.

Possible solutions:
1. Files that the application needs can be deployed with the application or put in Azure Storage. You can use Azure Storage File Shares as a drop-in replacement for on-premises file share.
2. Other services that the application depends on might need to be migrated to Azure, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.
3. If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premise, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.
Local OS environment access detected
 Potential 1
FilePosition
src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.csLine 56
src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.csLine 56

Explanation

Local OS environment access detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, Read config via App Settings or App Configuration; avoid machine‑specific environment APIs. Persist environment setup via install scripts when needed.

When running in Azure App Service environment, your application can read environment variables that you define in App Service settings. Using environment API other than reading environment variables might indicate that your application depends on some local machine's features and might be broken on App Service sandbox or not scale well. Review your scenarios and either refactor them to be more cloud friendly or choose the option in App Service to host your application in the sandbox for Windows Container Web Apps.

If you choose to use other Azure hosting options such as Azure Container Apps (ACA) or Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), environment APIs might work, however scaling still might be an issue.
SQL database connection detected
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\Web.config

Explanation

SQL database connection detected.

Ensure the database is available/reachable on Azure.

If it is not, there are multiple ways you can move your data to Azure:
1. Migrate to Azure SQL Database.
2. Consider Azure SQL Managed Instance if you need features that are not available in Azure SQL Database and you don’t want to use a VM.
3. Migrate your database servers directly to SQL Server on Azure VMs.

To assess database migration effort, you can use Azure Migrate tool, see the link below.

Explanation

Connection strings without configuration builders detected.

Keeping connection strings directly in the app is not the best practice and might introduce security risks, increased maintenance, scalability challenges or compliance standards (such as PCI DSS, GDPR, etc.).

Instead, it is recommended to use configuration builders to get secrets from secure sources in Azure environment.

Your current approach of serving static content directly might lead to increased costs, performance issues, maintenance challenges (requiring application redeployment for content changes), and security risks.

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience
 Optional 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\eShopWCFService.csproj

Explanation

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, validate on .NET Framework 4.8 or move to .NET 10. Persist any runtime prerequisites via install scripts; test in staging before production.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

Application targeting .NET framework lower than 4.7.1 might missing features that would be needed for some cloud scenarios like scaling or getting secrets from secure external sources.

Azure App Service runs apps on .NET Framework 4.8 or .NET Framework 3.5. Apps running on on .NET Framework versions older than .NET Framework 4.8 could have potential compatibility issues. It is recommended to test your application running on .NET Framework 4.8. Note that it is not necessary to re-target to .NET Framework 4.8, only to validate that the app correctly runs on that version of .NET Framework.

In the long term it is also recommended to upgrade your application to latest supported .NET 8+ which would significantly increase performance of your application. Use tools like .NET Upgrade Assistant to help with upgrading your application to newer .NET.
System.Data.SqlClient dependency detected
 Optional 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\Web.config

Explanation

System.Data.SqlClient dependency is detected.

While System.Data.SqlClient will work in Azure, the newer Microsoft.Data.SqlClient package is the primary .NET SQL client moving forward and receiving the latest features. For example, Microsoft.Data.SqlClient easily allows use of Azure Managed Identity from a connection string.

Project's target framework(s) needs to be changed
 Mandatory 1
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\eShopWCFService.csproj
src\eShopWinForms\eShopWinForms.csproj

Explanation

Project's target framework(s) needs to be changed to the new target framework that you selected for this upgrade.

During upgrade target framework will be adjusted to corresponding platform when applicable. In some cases project would result in multiple target frameworks after the upgrade if it was using features that now have their own platforms in modern .NET frameworks (windows, iOS, Android etc).
Project file needs to be converted to SDK-style
 Mandatory 1
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\eShopWCFService.csproj

Explanation

Project file needs to be converted to SDK-style. Modern .NET framework projects require a change in the project file format and use SDK corresponding to project flavor and functionality.
WCF Client APIs
 Mandatory 1
FilePosition

Explanation

WCF client-side APIs for building service clients that communicate with WCF services. These APIs are available as exact equivalents via NuGet packages - add System.ServiceModel.* NuGet packages (System.ServiceModel.Http, System.ServiceModel.Primitives, System.ServiceModel.NetTcp, etc.)
Legacy Configuration System
 Mandatory 2
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy XML-based configuration system (app.config/web.config) that has been replaced by a more flexible configuration model in .NET Core. The old system was rigid and XML-based. Migrate to Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration with JSON/environment variables; use System.Configuration.ConfigurationManager NuGet package as interim bridge if needed.
GDI+ / System.Drawing
 Mandatory 1
FilePosition

Explanation

System.Drawing APIs for 2D graphics, imaging, and printing that are available via NuGet package System.Drawing.Common. Note: Not recommended for server scenarios due to Windows dependencies; consider cross-platform alternatives like SkiaSharp or ImageSharp for new code.
Windows Forms Legacy Controls
 Mandatory 3
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy Windows Forms controls that have been removed from .NET Core/5+ including StatusBar, DataGrid, ContextMenu, MainMenu, MenuItem, and ToolBar. These controls were replaced by more modern alternatives. Use ToolStrip, MenuStrip, ContextMenuStrip, and DataGridView instead.
Windows Forms
 Mandatory 1

Data Storage & External Services

One service-owned SQL Server database stores catalog, stock and promotion data. Compose supplies SQL Server, while the non-container connection is selected through the service configuration; connection strings are intentionally redacted in the companion inventory. Product images are client-local files, not database blobs or an image service [A6–A9]. No broker, external business API or distributed cache was identified in the scoped source/manifests.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • The client uses view events and a manually constructed controller/proxy, not an active DI container. ApplicationModule.Load contains commented registration examples only [A3, A10].
  • The service directly uses an EF DbContext; no separate repository/business-service boundary exists in the active call chain [A5, A6].
  • Server entity classes also define SOAP data contracts; the client uses generated mutable copies [A4, A5]. Source declares differing server/client runtimes; successful interoperability was not verified.

DTOs & Contracts

CatalogItem, CatalogBrand, CatalogType, CatalogItemsStock and DiscountItem are service-level mutable data contracts, reused as persistence models. CatalogItem and stock objects are mutation requests; the same types and collections are responses. There are no immutable request records or gateway-owned composition DTOs. The generated proxy duplicates contracts through DataContract/DataMember XML serialization and maps server lists to client arrays [S1, S3]. Entity fields and persistence relationships are documented in data-architecture.md.

No OpenAPI, protobuf or GraphQL schema was found in the scoped files. WCF metadata and the generated SOAPAction declarations are the available contract evidence, not a checked-in authoritative WSDL snapshot.

Communication Patterns

  • Synchronous: view/controller calls to a generated ClientBase proxy; service-to-EF direct calls [S2, S3, S6].
  • Async: generated Task APIs exist, but the handwritten controller calls synchronous methods. No broker/event bus, eventual-consistency mechanism, gateway or service-discovery client was found.
  • Composition: the desktop separately fetches catalog and active discount and combines them for display; it is not an API gateway [S2].
  • Resilience: no application retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead or fallback was found in the active path. Binding timeouts are not explicitly overridden; framework defaults apply, with effective runtime values unverified. The generated binding sets maximum message/buffer sizes and reader quotas to their maximums and permits cookies [S3].
  • Addressing: generated default proxy hardcodes localhost:5113. App.config carries a matching address, but the constructor actually selects the generated programmatic binding/address, not an XML configuration-name constructor [S3]. No client-side load balancing is evident.
  • Availability: SQL access is necessary for data operations; Compose ordering does not guarantee database readiness. See configuration-inventory.md.
  • Security posture: the explicit service endpoint is basicHttpBinding and the generated client uses HTTP with default BasicHttpBinding security, without credentials. No application authorization/role checks were identified. An HTTPS protocol mapping exists but neither forces TLS on this endpoint nor proves deployed TLS; IIS authentication outside these files is unknown [S3, S5, S6]. Exception detail in faults is disabled in service configuration [S5].

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. Published service artifacts and external nat network must exist before image/container startup [C6, C10].
  2. Compose starts sql.data before eshopwcfservice via short-form depends_on. The SQL container has a query-based healthcheck, but no service_healthy condition or explicit wait loop connects readiness to service startup [C6].
  3. Catalog operations require SQL connectivity. First database access can initialize and seed a missing database; there is no explicit startup probe or application retry [C12].
  4. The desktop constructs the proxy and performs initial requests before displaying the form; unavailable service/database can prevent initial loading. No degraded startup branch is implemented [C13].

No application health endpoint, readiness timeout or deployment orchestrator beyond Compose was identified. Effective IIS settings and platform health defaults are unknown.

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

Repository Compose literals → Docker environment → service Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable lookup → EF connection. A missing environment value falls back to the named XML connection [C12]. Core Business Workflows

Operators browse a product catalog with date-active promotional pricing, check availability for a chosen day and record dated stock quantities. The scoped code does not implement checkout, payment, orders or shipment fulfilment.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
CatalogItemCatalogService / catalogProduct offered for display and availability lookupBelongs to brand/type; referenced by stock
CatalogBrandCatalogService / catalogProduct brand groupingGroups catalog items
CatalogTypeCatalogService / catalogProduct category groupingGroups catalog items
CatalogItemsStockCatalogService / inventoryAvailable quantity for an item on a particular calendar dayLogical item reference; persistence caveat in data-architecture.md
DiscountItemCatalogService / promotionsDate-bounded promotion applied to displayed catalog pricesGlobal, not linked to a particular product

These are descriptive subdomains within one service, not independently deployed bounded contexts or separate DDD aggregates [B1, B2].

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
CatalogServiceCatalog, inventory and promotionsAll five domain entitiesOne database via EntityModel
Desktop controller/viewOperator experienceNo authoritative persisted entitiesSOAP service; local image assets

The server is the source of truth. The desktop receives generated contract copies and joins product and discount information for display, not separate domain-service responses [B3, B4].

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Initialize and browse the discounted catalog

  1. Program constructs the view, generated service client and controller, then loads data before displaying the modal form [B5].
  2. The controller looks up today's promotion for the banner, loads all catalog items and today's discount, loads brand/type choices, and fills the shipment item selector [B3].
  3. Changing either filter raises a view event. The controller reloads matching items, fetches today's discount again and passes both to the view [B3, B4].
  4. The view computes displayed prices under the Display discount rule and loads product images from local assets. No discounted price is persisted [B4].
  5. With no matching promotion, items display with no reduction; transport or image-load errors have no implemented fallback in this path.

Workflow 2: Record dated stock availability

  1. Operator chooses an item and enters quantity/date. The Availability input guard runs in the view; parse failures are not caught [B4].
  2. Controller creates a stock contract and calls CreateAvailableStock [B3].
  3. Service searches for the same item and calendar day under the Daily overwrite rule. An existing record's quantity is replaced; otherwise a new record is allocated under the Manual identifier rule [B1].
  4. SaveChanges persists the result. Only after the service returns does the view show success and clear entry controls [B3, B4].

Although the UI calls the entry a shipment, it is not a shipment lifecycle: quantities are overwritten, not accumulated, and there is no receipt, reservation or dispatch state.

Workflow 3: Check stock for a calendar day

  1. Operator selects a product and a day; the view extracts its identifier from the selected label [B4].
  2. Controller requests availability. The service compares calendar dates under the Daily lookup rule [B1, B3].
  3. The integer result is appended to the view's result list. Zero does not distinguish a missing stock record from an explicit zero quantity.

Workflow 4: Provision initial catalog state

On first database access, an absent database is created and populated with reference values, products, stock and historic promotions [B6]. This is an initialization routine, not a recurring synchronization task; it does not update an existing database or refresh old promotion dates. No scheduler, event consumer or batch workflow was identified in scope.

Other contract-only catalog operations provide item find/create/update/delete. The examined desktop controller does not expose catalog-edit calls; those operations should not be presented as verified UI workflows [B1, B3].

Cross-Service Data Flows

The only application network boundary is desktop-to-CatalogService SOAP. The desktop separately obtains products and a date-active promotion, combines them locally and renders adjusted prices; brands/types populate independent selectors. Stock writes and reads use the same service and same underlying store [B1, B3].

There is no gateway, broker, cross-service saga, bulk remote aggregation or independent promotion service. No circuit breaker/fallback converts service failure into partial business results. A missing discount is a normal result, not a service-unavailability fallback. Generated Task methods are transport conveniences, not asynchronous business events [B7].

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant User as "Operator" participant View as "Stock entry view" participant Ctrl as "Desktop controller" participant Svc as "Catalog service" participant Stock as "Dated stock records" User->>View: Choose item and enter quantity and date alt Required input missing View-->>User: Return without submitting else Input present and parse succeeds View->>Ctrl: Availability event Ctrl->>Svc: Record dated stock quantity Svc->>Stock: Find same item and calendar day alt Existing daily record Svc->>Stock: Replace available quantity else No daily record Svc->>Stock: Allocate identifier and add record end Svc->>Stock: Save changes alt Persistence succeeds Stock-->>Svc: Saved Svc-->>Ctrl: Completed Ctrl->>View: Notify updated View-->>User: Success message and cleared inputs else Persistence or transport fails Note over View,Stock: No compensating action or user-facing fallback is implemented end end

Business Rules & Decision Logic

RuleActual behavior and limitationsEvidence
All-filter sentinelBrand/type identifier 0 means unrestricted; nonzero values filter by equality after materialization[B1, B3]
Active promotion selectionStart and end dates inclusive; ignores time of day; returns first matching record without ordering or overlap resolution[B1]
Display discount ruleDisplayed price = product price multiplied by one minus promotion Size; no promotion means Size 0. Banner percentage rounds Size times 100. Uses current desktop time; no timezone policy or stored discounted price[B3, B4]
Availability input guardMissing selected product, empty quantity or empty date silently returns. Otherwise int.Parse and Convert.ToDateTime are used without TryParse/error handling[B4]
Daily overwrite ruleFirst stock record for same item/date is replaced, not incremented. No explicit uniqueness constraint or concurrent upsert control was identified[B1, B2]
Daily lookup ruleFirst same-day matching stock record returns its quantity; missing match returns 0. No cumulative stock or carry-forward computation[B1]
Manual identifier ruleProduct Id and new StockId allocated using maximum existing value plus one; empty-set and concurrent creation cases have no explicit handling[B1]
Reference-value lengthBrand and type strings have StringLength(50). No explicit service validation invocation or business-level error translation; EF validation may apply at save[B2]
Missing range/domain checksNo positive-quantity requirement, price-range rule, discount-fraction range, promotion date-order check or item-existence check in stock service code[B1, B2, B4]
Selection prerequisiteStock search dereferences selected list item without a null guard; malformed/no selection can fail before a service call[B4]

Transactions: each mutation saves independently; no application transaction spans the initial lookup, identifier allocation and write. Database seeding saves each group separately. No compensation or distributed transaction behavior is implemented [B1, B6].

Error handling: null item/promotion and zero missing-stock results are explicit decisions; parse, transport, image and persistence failures are not translated to business errors in the active controller/view. RemoveCatalogItem passes the incoming entity directly to Remove without an explicit attach/find step, so disconnected-entity behavior is unverified rather than assumed successful [B1, B4].

Authorization and audit: no resource-owner/role checks, business audit events or durable change-history model was found in the active workflow code. External IIS/database policies are outside what these sources establish. There is no order/status state machine [B1–B4].

Generated-code boundary: the proxy and form designer are generated artifacts; the workflow decisions above are traced to handwritten controller, view, service and initializer code. The commented ApplicationModule registration and unused server-side client stub are not alternate active workflows [B5, B7].

Version & Compatibility Risks

The server targets an out-of-support .NET Framework version (4.6.1), and the active desktop target .NET 6 is also out of support as of this assessment. This is a declared-dependency inventory, not an upgrade assessment. The active client is explicitly Windows-targeted [D1]; compatibility findings produced for a non-Windows target cannot establish that its Windows Forms APIs require rewrites. Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

Five EF6 entity sets persist catalog, brand, type, dated stock and discount data to SQL Server. This is a source-derived model, not a verified live schema.

Database Configuration

Service/ModuleDB TypeProfileDriverConnectionMigration Tool
eShopWCFServiceSQL ServerLocal/defaultSystem.Data.SqlClient and EF6 SqlServer providerNamed configuration fallback; full string redactedCreateDatabaseIfNotExists initializer; no versioned migrations found
eShopWCFServiceSQL Server Windows Developer containerCompose overrideSame providerEnvironment override; full string redactedSame code initializer

Connection precedence and raw setting names belong to configuration-inventory.md. EF registers the initializer when constructing EntityModel [P1, P2]. It creates/seeds absent databases rather than migrating an existing schema. Seed order is types, brands, products, stock, discounts; each helper saves separately [P3]. Seed data includes 12 items, five brands, four types, six stock rows and six date-bounded discounts, with dates in 2017 [P4]. No explicit pool tuning, SQL schema-version scripts or deployed encryption policy was identified.

All entities are owned by eShopWCFService. The item-to-stock edge is a logical relationship used by service queries, not proof of an EF/database FK: stock has an integer item identifier but no navigation property or explicit relationship configuration [P5, P7]. Product-to-brand/type navigations are unidirectional, with no inverse collections. Required integer references imply required relationships by EF convention; generated schema and cascade behavior were not inspected.

Caching Strategy

No Redis, MemoryCache, distributed cache, explicit query-result cache or configured EF second-level cache was found. DbContext tracking is per context, not an application caching policy. There are no application TTL, eviction or cache-region settings to inventory. Client arrays and controls hold loaded results but do not establish a reusable cache.

Data Ownership Boundaries

A single service reads and writes the same catalog database: no database-per-domain partition, CQRS store separation, outbox or cross-service database joins were identified. The desktop receives SOAP contracts, not direct database access. Brand/type enrichment occurs inside CatalogService; discount/catalog display composition occurs in the desktop [P7, P8]. The unused HiLo helper does not prove that its sequence is provisioned or used.
